title: Chapter 114 – Winter Cold
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

Two weeks later.

On the thirty-first night of the frost, the Spring Vein stops.

Jian feels it go at the hour of the rat, lying awake on his cot in the Pill Hall's spare alcove with a quilt up to his chin. It is not a pain. It is a silence. For eight years there has been a small low pulse in the gray scarred length of his left arm, a patient green hum, and in the cold months it has dwindled to a thread. Tonight, between one heartbeat and the next, the thread breaks. The arm lies on the quilt like a stranger's. He lifts it with the other hand, and it is heavy and cold and entirely without feeling, and when he presses a fingernail into the palm, nothing comes.

He lies there for a long time, looking at the ceiling.

Dormant, he tells himself. Not dead. It woke in the spring last year, after the freeze. It will wake again.

But the register, when he asks it in the Dock at dawn, is blunt.

```
OPERATOR ARK-7 :: STATUS
SPRING VEIN: DORMANT (DEEP FROST, -9 C)
INTEGRITY 58%. NO DRAW POSSIBLE UNTIL ABOVE FREEZING.
FORECAST: FROST CONTINUES 40+ DAYS.
CE INCOME: LABOR ONLY (2/NIGHT, CAP 6/WEEK).
CE: 18
```

Eighteen. He has not earned a point since the envoy. The nights have been taken by other work, and the work has not paid.

He closes the panel and stands for a time in the cold air of the Dock, with the lamp burning steady on the wall and the blank steel of the door at his back. He is twenty-eight. He is a Foundation Middle. He is an Operator of a machine older than the Sect, and he has eighteen points of a currency no one else can see, and two weeks left on a stolen reprieve, and his mother's name on a sheet of plum-bark in his sleeve.

And I cannot draw a single breath of green.

* * *

Hu brings the blades to the Garden Hall on the morning of the first great snow.

He carries them in an oilcloth roll, as he carries everything, and sets them down on the study table with the tenderness of a man putting down infants. There are three. Short, plain, dark, with no ornament but a faint spiral etched at the guard. They are the quiet blades forged in the Veiled Forge nine months ago, and Hu has spent every night since polishing them. In the lamplight they look like long thumbs of slate.

"The first is Feng's," he says. "The second is Bei's. The third I'll hold myself." He turns one over. "They'll mute a Qi form inside twenty paces. Not kill it. Mute it. Anything born of cultivation, a talisman, a blade-light, a shade, it'll go dull in the radius and stay dull as long as the blade is drawn. Uses nothing. Takes nothing. It's just a hole."

"A hole in the Qi."

"A hole." Hu's heavy face creases. "The worst thing I've ever made. And the one I'm proudest of."

Feng reaches for his and does not draw it. He only lifts it, and sets it back, and looks at his brother.

"You think they will come to the stair," he says.

"I think they came to the stair last night."

"The footprints."

"They were not made by a man." Jian has told no one this but Qin Hao. "I looked at them with—" He stops. "I looked closely. They had no weight. They were pressed into the snow by something that did not touch it."

"A shade."

"A Registry Blood Shadow. A small one. A scout." He lays his hand flat on the table. "It was counting. That is what they do. They count who goes in and out of the stair, and when, and who stands guard. Then they send the larger ones."

"How many?"

"I do not know."

Nobody speaks. Kuang, in the doorway, lifts her iron bar an inch and sets it down again, as she does before a bout, and says only: "Two watches. They will come at the third." She is never wrong about such things. Outside, the snow falls on the cloister roofs in thick slow flakes. The Garden's last green has been buried since the third night, and the lane is a canal of white. Behind them, in the long bright room, Wenyuan's brush has stopped moving over the muster.

"Then I will stand the stair," says Feng.

"No."

"Yes."

"You are a Foundation Middle. You are the best swordsman in the clan. You are the second reason there is a clan. I will not put you in front of something I cannot see."

"You are not putting me anywhere." His brother says it without anger. "I have stood that stair for six years. I carried the Gate Bearer's tablet up it on my back. It is mine as much as yours. If something comes, I will be there, with Kuang and Bei and a hole in my hand, and you will be under the ground with a door shut behind you, where I can't be asked to explain myself."

Jian opens his mouth.

"Brother," says Feng, and for a moment, in the scarred square face, there is no stubbornness at all. "Let me."

He lets him.

* * *

The Zhao men arrive at the Garden that afternoon, nine of them, led by Yao.

They come up the lane in a file through the new snow, in the plain brown of Garden guards, with the sleeves of their short robes tied back and their breath smoking. Yao is twenty-one now and has lost the hunted look of the boy who carried a stolen key; he walks at the head of the line with his shoulders square and a quiet blade strapped across his back, and when he reaches the gate he stops and bows to Wenyuan as a steward bows to his lord.

"The Zhao muster stands ready," he says. "Forty-three, of whom nine are fit to hold a line. The rest will hold the walls."

"We have been asked to stay out of the Sect's quarrel," says Wenyuan mildly.

"We have been asked," says Yao, "by people who burned our house." He looks past the old man into the cloister, where Hui, fourteen and thin, is feeding a brazier under Yue's solemn eye. "I did not come to take orders. I came to say that the Zhao are yours, and that wherever the stair is, we are."

Wenyuan studies him. Then he steps aside, and the file of men goes in beneath the lintel, and the Garden Hall, for the first time in its short life, is a place with a garrison.

Jian watches from the cloister. He thinks: two hundred and thirty-one, and nine to hold a line. He thinks of the number and of the four black shapes, and he does not let himself finish the sum.

* * *

It begins at the second watch.

The storm has been gathering all evening. At dusk the wind drops, and the sky goes a low sodden yellow, and the first big flakes come drifting out of nothing like feathers. By the first watch the stair is invisible. By the second the whole of the Gate Court is a blind white room with the lanterns at its corners gone to smudges, and the only sound in it is the soft, enormous hush of falling snow.

Jian is in the Dock.

He sits on the bench with his hands on his knees and his back to the lamp, facing the door, and he waits. He has told himself this is sensible. A man who goes up when the storm breaks will be seen and killed. A man who stays below, behind a lock that no hand but his can open, will survive. The Door in Autumn is closed, saving its points, and the register hums, and the lamp burns, and above his head, through three feet of stone, he can hear nothing.

At the third watch, the lock rings.

Not the lock. The bell. The little bronze bell above the Gate stair, the one that rings itself when the stair is crossed, gives a single high clear note, and then a second, and then it falls silent, as though a hand had been laid on its tongue.

He is on his feet.

They are here.

He does not decide. He goes up the stair.

* * *

The Gate Court is a cauldron of white and black.

He comes out of the stair mouth into a wind that has risen like a wall, a shrieking, whirling, solid thing that drives the snow into his eyes in handfuls, and for a moment he is blind. Then he opens the Door in Autumn, and the storm falls open like a curtain.

It costs two points. He has eighteen.

He sees the court laid out in bright cold lines, as one sees a map. The lanterns are three bright smears. The stair lies behind him. And across the whole breadth of the court, in a half circle, standing in the deep unbroken snow with their feet leaving no mark, are shapes.

Four of them.

They are tall, thin, and entirely black, like men cut out of a night sky with a pair of shears. They have no faces, only smooth ovals of darkness where a face should be. They have hands, long, with too many joints, and each carries, pinned to the center of its chest, a small square tag of white bark. A number is inked on each tag in a neat clerk's hand. Nine. Fourteen. Twenty. Twenty-two.

Registry Blood Shadows, he thinks. Rill-grade. Four.

Between them and the stair stand three figures in the snow.

Kuang is on the left, in a short padded robe, with her iron bar planted upright before her like a flagstaff. Her flat eyes are narrowed to slits and the wind is whipping her cropped hair across her scar. On the right is Bei, enormous, bareheaded, wrapped to the neck in a bearskin, holding his quiet blade in a fist the size of a shovel. And in the center, very still, with the dark blade held low and ready and the snow gathering on his shoulders, stands Feng.

Hu is behind them, a pace back, with the third blade.

Nobody has moved. Nobody speaks. The snow comes down between the two lines like a curtain of white thread.

Then the shadow marked Nine lifts its head and tilts it, as a bird does, and the four of them begin to walk.

* * *

The quiet blades work.

Jian sees it the instant the first shadow crosses into the circle. The black shape is flowing across the snow, smooth as ink, silent as a thought. At twenty paces it slows. At fifteen it falters. At ten it shudders, like a candle in a draft, and its edges begin to blur, and a thin gray steam rises from its shoulders as the Qi that holds it together begins to come apart.

Yes, he thinks fiercely. Hu. You old fool. You did it.

Feng steps forward and meets it.

It is a clean, short thing. The dark blade rises and falls. The shadow throws up an arm and the arm unravels, like wet paper, and the quiet blade passes through the place where a heart would be and comes out the other side, and Nine falls apart into a stain of gray mist that the wind takes before it hits the ground.

One.

The others do not hesitate.

Fourteen and Twenty come together, and the field shudders. Kuang takes the left, and the iron bar rings against something that is not metal, and her whole big body swings with it in a short brutal arc. Bei takes the right. The bearskin flies. He roars, a wordless huge sound, and drives his blade up under the arm of Twenty, and the shadow bursts. Hu, behind them, shouts something. The wind swallows it. Twenty, as it dies, claws at his shoulder; the bearskin tears; and Bei laughs, a short wild bark of a laugh, because he has never in his life been so glad of a cold winter's night, and a thing that can be hit.

And it is going well, for fifteen heartbeats, it is going very well.

Then Jian sees it.

The last shadow, Twenty-two, has not come with the rest. It has gone round. While the other three were walking straight at the line, it slid sideways through the snow along the wall of the court, outside the blades' radius, along the edge of the circle where the dull zone ends, and now it stands at the stair mouth, three paces from Jian, a tall black shape with a hole where its face should be.

It raises one long hand.

The lock, he thinks. It wants the lock.

He moves.

He does not think about what he can do. One Seam Needle is left in his belt, the last of a batch printed two winters ago, a thin silver-black pin no longer than his finger, and he draws it and throws. The price comes out of him like breath: six points, gone in a heartbeat, and the cold of it runs up his arm to the shoulder. It leaves his hand with a sound like tearing silk. It crosses the three paces in no time at all and enters the hole where the face should be, and the shadow stops.

It stops completely, as a clock does.

For one breath it stands there, frozen, a black shape pinned in the white. Then the thing begins to unravel from the head down, in long shuddering ribbons, and the tag on its chest curls and burns and falls to ash in the snow.

And from the unraveling, as it goes, comes a voice.

It is a small voice, and it is not a shadow's. It is a man's, thin, hoarse, and terribly tired. It says four words, quite clearly, as though speaking from a very great distance.

"Tell Seventeen I'm sorry."

Then it is gone, and there is only snow.

* * *

He does not understand until he turns.

Feng is on his knees in the snow, ten paces from the stair.

He has dropped the quiet blade. It lies beside him, a dark thumb in the white. He is clutching his left shoulder with his right hand, and between his fingers, black and slow, something is welling up that is not blood. It spreads under his palm like ink in water. It crawls up his neck. It climbs the side of his jaw in a fine dark web of veins, and his face, in the light of the broken lantern, is the color of tallow.

"It was Fourteen," says Kuang flatly. She has reached him first. "It was not dead. It came back up from the snow. It touched him once."

"I felt nothing," says Feng, in a puzzled voice. "It did not hurt. It only— went cold."

Jian is already on his knees beside him. He catches the heavy shoulder, tears the short robe from the neck, and sees the mark. A hand-print in black, as if burned, the fingers spread, pressed into the skin above the collarbone. And from the print, spreading in every direction, thin dark threads of rot, creeping down the arm, across the chest, up the throat.

"Bei," he says. "Take his feet. Hu, the cloak. We are going to the Pill Hall."

"It's all right," Feng says. His voice is slurred. "It's only a shoulder."

"Be quiet."

"Jian—"

"Be quiet. Please."

His brother looks up at him. The black web has reached the corner of his eye. In its light, the familiar square face looks suddenly very young.

"I held the stair," he says.

"You did."

"I wanted you to see." His eyes close. "That it could be held."

* * *

Qin Hao arrives at the Pill Hall when the work is half done.

He stands in the doorway of the big treatment room in a snow-crusted cloak, with his beard white and his hands knotted behind him, and does not speak. Behind him in the corridor the apprentices are running with bowls. In front of him, on the long stone table under the hanging lamps, Bai bends over a motionless form with a knife in one hand and a bowl of something that smokes in the other.

Feng lies on his back. His chest rises and falls in a slow shallow rhythm. His left shoulder is bare, and the black mark on it has been cut open in a neat cross and packed with a glowing paste that stinks of camphor and burnt hair. Kuang holds his head. Bei holds his legs. Wenyuan, ashen, holds his hand.

And Jian stands at the table's foot with his own hands hanging, because there is nothing he is allowed to do.

"Four," says Qin Hao at last, very low. "Registry Blood Shadows, all four, on my stair. I was on the ridge. I heard the bell." He looks at the table. "I came as fast as I could."

"You came," says Jian. "It was enough."

"It was not." The old man's face does not change. "I should have posted more. I should have known the Gate would be tested before the solstice. I told myself the cold would hold them."

"It held them for five weeks."

"It held them until they had counted us."

Jian looks at the cloth wrapped round his own knuckles. "The last one spoke," he says. "When it came apart. It said, Tell Seventeen I'm sorry."

The old man's head turns slowly.

"Seventeen."

"Yan Zhi was Seventeen. He told me so himself, in the House's own words, the night he left it." He keeps his voice level. "Someone inside that shape knew him. Someone who was a man once, and is a number now, and is still sorry."

"Then it was not a shade," says Qin Hao.

"It was a Number, worn like a glove." Jian's jaw tightens. "They are not summoning shadows from nothing. They are making them out of their own."

Neither of them says what that means. In the corridor outside, somewhere, a bowl clatters and a girl's voice calls for more hot water, and the sound is small and ordinary and very far away.

Bai grunts. He sets the bowl down and straightens, wiping the knife on his apron, and for the first time Jian sees how old he looks: gray in the lamplight, with his round face gone slack and the plum in his belt untouched.

"Well," says the old man.

Nobody answers.

"I'll tell you what I can. The Shadow's mark is a Rill-grade Blood Shadow's mark. I've seen it twice. Once on a sick calf and once on a dead man. It doesn't kill outright. It eats the meridians from the inside, one channel at a time, like rot in a plum." He chews, slowly. "I've cut out the worst of it. The arm is saved. The man is saved. He'll wake tomorrow and want his supper."

"But?" says Wenyuan, hoarsely.

"But three channels in that shoulder are black to the root, and two more are cracked. They run to the Foundation seat. I can burn the rot out, but I can't burn the channels back." Bai meets the father's eyes. "He was Foundation Middle at the start of the night. By the morning he'll hold Foundation Early, if he's lucky, and he won't hold it steady. It's a thing that can be mended, in time, with the right medicine and a lot of patience. A year. Two."

Wenyuan makes a small sound.

"He'll live," says Bai, gently. "That's the thing. He'll live, and he'll walk, and he'll pick up a sword. But he's lost a step, and the step will cost the clan two years."

* * *

Wenyuan finds him in the corridor an hour later, sitting on the cold bench with his head against the wall.

His father does not sit. He stands in front of him in the stained gray robe he has worn for two days, a tall, stooped, tired man with a trace of ink still on his thumb, and looks at the lamp-lit door of the treatment room. For a time neither says anything.

"Bai says two years," says Wenyuan finally.

"Yes."

"I said to him: I would give twenty." His voice cracks, once, and steadies. "He said it does not work that way."

"I am sorry."

"Do not be sorry. Be honest." Wenyuan lowers himself onto the bench. He sits like a man whose knees have begun to remind him of every winter. "I do not know what the envoy offered you, Jian. Your mother does not say, and Ye will not, and I have not asked. I have only watched you for nine days, and I think I understand a little."

"Father—"

"I will not tell you to take it. I will not tell you to refuse it." He puts one big dry hand on his son's knee. "When I was a boy in the Orchard, my father told me that a house is not its walls or its roll. A house is the thing it will not sell. I did not understand it. I thought it was a saying." He breathes out. "We have sold a good many things, you and I. A tutor. A forge. A year of your life, or two. I think we may be coming to the end of what can be sold."

"And if the price is the Gate?"

"Then the Gate is not ours to sell." His father's eyes are red-rimmed and steady. "And if the price is your name, I do not know whether we have the right to pay it for you. I only know that your mother will go on loving whatever walks out of that stair, and so will I."

Jian cannot answer. He puts his head back against the cold wall and shuts his eyes, and the old hand stays on his knee, warm and heavy, as it did when he was four.

* * *

Dawn comes slowly, a cold gray smear along the east.

Jian stands at the window of the treatment room and watches the snow stop. The wind has gone. The court is a smooth bright sheet, scarred by a few black stains and a line of footprints where the porters are coming to clear it. On the table behind him his brother sleeps, gray-faced, breathing evenly, with his father's hand in his.

The envoy's paper is in his sleeve. He has not taken it out. He does not need to.

Kept, it said. Twelve names. Twelve times that word, in a clerk's smooth hand, and a deadline at midwinter.

He had thought he understood what it was telling him. He had thought it was a promise, or a bribe. A bargain to be weighed. It had not occurred to him until now that it was also a measurement, that someone was holding a ruler against the Lin clan, and had chosen tonight to show him where the ruler ended.

I did not choose, he thinks. And they have shown me what not choosing costs.

A sound behind him.

It is Yue, standing in the doorway, in her night-robe, with a lamp. She is fifteen, and very white. She does not look at the table. She crosses the room and sets the lamp on the sill, and then, without a word, she opens her fist and lays something on the stone beside it.

A card. Small. Square. Creamy plum-bark, rough to the touch, with a black seal in the corner.

"It was on his pillow," she says. "When they brought him in. Under his hand."

He picks it up.

There are two lines, in the same fine hand. The first has been crossed out with a single stroke of red.

Lin Feng: Kept.

And below it, in black, newly written, the ink still faintly wet:

Lin Feng: Not yet.
